title: Imagination is More Important Than Knowledge
author: Houston, Parker
summary: Parker Houston argues that imagination, not accumulated knowledge, is the leadership trait most at risk of atrophy with age, and the one most necessary for sustained motivation and growth. Drawing on neuroimaging claims that aging brains shift from imagination-driven to memory-driven cognition, he frames the loss of a leader's creative capacity as a slow, largely invisible decline rather than a sudden failure. He supports the argument with a mix of leadership folklore (John Wooden writing bestsellers into his nineties, John Maxwell's dedicated weekly thinking time) and a cited Frontiers in Psychology claim from Harvard psychologist Brendan Gaessar that imagining an outcome measurably shifts its perceived and actual likelihood. The piece closes with five concrete practices for keeping imagination alive as a leader: protecting unstructured thinking time, changing physical environment, anchoring dreams to a stated purpose, keeping a written dream list, and deliberately surrounding oneself with other people who dream ambitiously rather than with reflexive skeptics.
points: Houston claims neuroimaging shows the aging brain shifts from operating out of imagination toward operating out of memory, framing declining creativity as a physiological drift leaders must actively resist.

He cites a Frontiers in Psychology paper by Harvard psychologist Brendan Gaessar claiming imagination affects the perceived and actual likelihood of an event occurring, used to justify practices like an annual written Life Plan.
John Wooden is offered as a counter-example of sustained creative output, having written several bestselling books into his late eighties and early nineties after retiring from coaching.
Leadership author John Maxwell's practice of blocking 2-4 hours of weekly unstructured thinking time is cited as the source of over 100 of his leadership books.

The piece prescribes five concrete habits for leaders: scheduled open thinking time, physical change of environment, purpose-anchored goals, a written dream list, and deliberately surrounding oneself with other ambitious dreamers rather than skeptics.
quotes: But modern neuroimaging suggests that as we age-the cognitive centers of our brain shift from living out of imagination-to living out of memory.
Without imagination Columbus never would have set out on his long journey, Steve Jobs never would have invented the iPhone, and Elon Musk would not be trying to get us to Mars.

Consider John Wooden-arguably one of the most successful coaches of all time. He passed away in 2010 just shy of his 100th birthday. After he retired from coaching, he wasn't done with his dreams. He wrote several of his bestselling books in his late eighties and early nineties!
An article published in Frontiers in Psychology by Harvard psychology professor Brendan Gaessar states, "research shows imagination influences the perceived and actual likelihood an event occurs.
I once heard John Maxwell say that he carves out 2-4 hours every week of thinking time. Out of his dedicated creative time flowed over 100 leadership books.

Your dreams don't grow legs around nay-sayers and fear mongers. These people will help you find every reason NOT to do something. And your social environment is one of the most powerful predictors for who you become, and life is way too short to succumb to the gravity of those that don't dream big.
